title: Radioactivity
seo_title: Secondary 4 Physics: Radioactivity Worksheets (O-Level 6091 with Answers)
standard_text: Describe the structure of an atom in terms of a nucleus of protons and neutrons with electrons around it; use nuclide notation (proton number Z, nucleon number A) and explain the term isotope; show awareness of background radiation and its sources; describe the nature, ionising effect and penetrating power of alpha, beta and gamma emissions; write nuclear equations for alpha and beta decay; define half-life and use it in calculations, including with decay data; describe uses of radioactivity and the precautions needed; describe nuclear fission and fusion (summary of the Singapore-Cambridge O-Level Physics 6091 syllabus).
meta_desc: Free Secondary 4 O-Level Physics worksheets on radioactivity: nuclide notation, isotopes, alpha, beta and gamma radiation, nuclear equations, half-life, uses and safety. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Half-life: the time for half the nuclei to decay.
key_sub: Alpha: Z − 2, A − 4. Beta: Z + 1, A unchanged.
body_html:
How to think about it

Unstable nuclei decay randomly and emit radiation.

  • Nuclide notation AZX: Z = protons, A = protons + neutrons. Isotopes have the same Z but different numbers of neutrons.
  • Alpha (He nucleus): most ionising, stopped by paper. Beta (electron): stopped by a few mm of aluminium. Gamma (EM wave): most penetrating, reduced by lead.
  • Alpha decay: A − 4, Z − 2. Beta decay: A unchanged, Z + 1.
  • After n half-lives, (1/2)ⁿ of the nuclei remain. Subtract background radiation before halving counts.
Example

Ra-226 (Z = 88) emits an alpha particle. New nucleus?

A = 226 − 4

Z = 88 − 2

Answer: radon-222 (Z = 86)

Example

80 g, half-life 6 days. Mass left after 18 days?

18 ÷ 6 = 3 half-lives

80 ÷ 2³

Answer: 10 g

Common mistakes

  • Thinking nothing is left after two half-lives. A quarter is left.
  • Saying gamma is the most ionising. Alpha is.
  • Lowering the proton number in beta decay. It rises by 1.
  • Forgetting to subtract the background count.

faq.q: How do you calculate with half-life?
faq.a: Count the number of half-lives that have passed, then halve the amount (or count rate) that many times. Subtract background radiation first.

faq.q: What stops alpha, beta and gamma radiation?
faq.a: Alpha is stopped by paper or a few cm of air, beta by a few mm of aluminium, and gamma is reduced by thick lead or concrete.

faq.q: What happens to the nucleus in alpha and beta decay?
faq.a: Alpha decay: the nucleon number falls by 4 and the proton number by 2. Beta decay: a neutron turns into a proton, so the proton number rises by 1 and the nucleon number is unchanged.

items.q: How many neutrons are in the nucleus <sup>23</sup><sub>11</sub>Na?
items.e: Neutrons = A − Z = 23 − 11 = 12.

items.q: How many electrons are in a neutral atom of <sup>3</sup><sub>1</sub>H?
items.e: A neutral atom has as many electrons as protons: 1.

items.q: What is nuclear fusion?
c: the decay of a nucleus by alpha emission
the joining of two light nuclei to form a heavier nucleus, releasing energy
the splitting of a heavy nucleus
items.e: It powers the Sun.

items.q: Why is ionising radiation harmful to living cells?
c: It can damage DNA, killing cells or causing mutations that may lead to cancer.
items.e: Ionisation breaks molecules.

items.q: What is the nucleon number of the nucleus <sup>90</sup><sub>38</sub>Sr?
items.e: The nucleon number (top number) A = protons + neutrons = 90.

items.q: <sup>32</sup><sub>15</sub>P decays to <sup>32</sup><sub>16</sub>S. What type of decay is this?
items.e: Compare the mass numbers and atomic numbers.

items.q: How many electrons are in a neutral atom of <sup>226</sup><sub>88</sub>Ra?
items.e: A neutral atom has as many electrons as protons: 88.

items.q: <sup>210</sup><sub>84</sub>Po (polonium) undergoes alpha decay. What nucleus forms?
items.e: Alpha decay: mass number −4, atomic number −2.

items.q: What is the nucleon number of the nucleus <sup>238</sup><sub>92</sub>U?
items.e: The nucleon number (top number) A = protons + neutrons = 238.

items.q: How many neutrons are in the nucleus <sup>235</sup><sub>92</sub>U?
items.e: Neutrons = A − Z = 235 − 92 = 143.

items.q: What happens to the proton number in alpha decay?
items.e: The nucleon number decreases by 4.

items.q: Which is a natural source of background radiation?
c: radon gas from rocks and soil
items.e: Cosmic rays and food are other natural sources.

items.q: <sup>234</sup><sub>90</sub>Th decays to <sup>234</sup><sub>91</sub>Pa. What type of decay is this?
items.e: Compare the mass numbers and atomic numbers.

items.q: How many protons are in the nucleus <sup>14</sup><sub>6</sub>C?
items.e: The proton number (lower number) is 6.

items.q: How many neutrons are in the nucleus <sup>137</sup><sub>55</sub>Cs?
items.e: Neutrons = A − Z = 137 − 55 = 82.

items.q: What is the nucleon number of the nucleus <sup>60</sup><sub>27</sub>Co?
items.e: The nucleon number (top number) A = protons + neutrons = 60.

items.q: How many protons are in the nucleus <sup>23</sup><sub>11</sub>Na?
items.e: The proton number (lower number) is 11.

items.q: What is nuclear fission?
c: the splitting of a large nucleus (such as uranium-235) into two smaller nuclei, releasing energy and neutrons
items.e: Used in nuclear power stations.

items.q: What is background radiation?
c: radiation only from nuclear power stations
low-level radiation that is always present from natural and artificial sources
items.e: Subtract it from readings.

items.q: How many neutrons are in the nucleus <sup>40</sup><sub>19</sub>K?
items.e: Neutrons = A − Z = 40 − 19 = 21.

items.q: Why is a beta source used to control the thickness of paper, rather than alpha or gamma?
c: Alpha would be stopped by the paper and gamma would pass through almost unchanged; beta's count changes with thickness.
items.e: The detector reading controls the rollers.

items.q: How ionising is gamma radiation?
items.e: Ionising power: alpha > beta > gamma.

items.q: What is needed to absorb most gamma radiation?
c: a few cm of air or a sheet of paper
several cm of lead or thick concrete (reduced, not completely)
items.e: Penetration: alpha < beta < gamma.

items.q: Which change can alter the half-life of a radioactive isotope?
c: none: heating, cooling and pressure do not change it
items.e: Half-life is a property of the nucleus.

items.q: What are isotopes?
c: atoms with different numbers of protons
atoms of the same element with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons
atoms of different elements with the same mass
items.e: Carbon-12 and carbon-14.

items.q: How ionising is beta radiation?
items.e: Ionising power: alpha > beta > gamma.

items.q: What is the relative charge of gamma radiation?
items.e: Alpha +2, beta −1, gamma 0 (uncharged).

items.q: Carbon-14 has a half-life of about 5700 years. A wooden tool has 1/4 of the carbon-14 of living wood. How old is it?
items.e: 1/4 means 2 half-lives.

items.q: What is the relative charge of an alpha particle?
items.e: Alpha +2, beta −1, gamma 0 (uncharged).

items.q: Radiation from a source passes through paper but is stopped by 3 mm of aluminium. What is it?
items.e: Alpha would be stopped by the paper; gamma would pass the aluminium.

items.q: Which radiation is the most penetrating?
items.e: Gamma rays are uncharged and weakly ionising.

items.q: A nucleus emits a gamma ray. What happens to its proton and nucleon numbers?
c: Z falls by 2 and A falls by 4.
items.e: Gamma emission only removes energy.

items.q: What is needed to absorb most beta radiation?
c: a few cm of air or a sheet of paper
several cm of lead or thick concrete (reduced, not completely)
items.e: Penetration: alpha < beta < gamma.

items.q: What is beta radiation?
c: a fast-moving electron from the nucleus
electromagnetic radiation of very short wavelength
items.e: Alpha: He nucleus. Beta: electron. Gamma: EM wave.

items.q: What is radioactive decay?
c: the splitting of every atom at once
a chemical reaction of a metal
the random, spontaneous emission of radiation from an unstable nucleus
the burning of a radioactive fuel
items.e: It cannot be speeded up by heating.

items.q: What is alpha radiation?
c: electromagnetic radiation of very short wavelength
a fast-moving electron from the nucleus
items.e: Alpha: He nucleus. Beta: electron. Gamma: EM wave.

items.q: What is the half-life of a radioactive isotope?
c: the time taken for half of the radioactive nuclei in a sample to decay
half the time for all the nuclei to decay
the time for the sample to lose half its mass of all substances
items.e: Each isotope has its own half-life.

items.q: What is the relative charge of a beta particle?
items.e: Alpha +2, beta −1, gamma 0 (uncharged).

items.q: Which radiation is stopped by a sheet of paper?
items.e: Alpha particles are large and highly ionising, so they lose energy quickly.

items.q: A detector reading barely changes when paper and then aluminium are placed in front of a source, but falls with thick lead. What does the source emit?
items.e: Only gamma gets through aluminium.

items.q: <sup>238</sup><sub>92</sub>U (uranium) undergoes alpha decay. What nucleus forms?
items.e: Alpha decay: mass number −4, atomic number −2.

items.q: A nucleus with mass number 24 and atomic number 11 emits a beta particle. What are the mass number and atomic number of the new nucleus?
items.e: Alpha: mass −4, atomic −2. Beta: a neutron becomes a proton, so atomic +1 and mass unchanged.

items.q: <sup>210</sup><sub>84</sub>Po decays by emitting an alpha particle. What nucleus is formed?
items.e: An alpha particle is <sup>4</sup><sub>2</sub>He: A falls by 4 and Z falls by 2, giving <sup>206</sup><sub>82</sub>Pb.

items.q: <sup>241</sup><sub>95</sub>Am decays by emitting an alpha particle. What nucleus is formed?
items.e: An alpha particle is <sup>4</sup><sub>2</sub>He: A falls by 4 and Z falls by 2, giving <sup>237</sup><sub>93</sub>Np.

items.q: <sup>24</sup><sub>11</sub>Na decays by emitting a beta particle. What nucleus is formed?
items.e: In beta decay a neutron becomes a proton and an electron is emitted: A stays the same and Z rises by 1, giving <sup>24</sup><sub>12</sub>Mg.

items.q: A nucleus with mass number 90 and atomic number 38 emits a beta particle. What are the mass number and atomic number of the new nucleus?
items.e: Alpha: mass −4, atomic −2. Beta: a neutron becomes a proton, so atomic +1 and mass unchanged.

items.q: <sup>131</sup><sub>53</sub>I (iodine) undergoes beta decay. What nucleus forms?
items.e: Beta decay: mass number same, atomic number +1.

items.q: <sup>222</sup><sub>86</sub>Rn decays by emitting an alpha particle. What nucleus is formed?
items.e: An alpha particle is <sup>4</sup><sub>2</sub>He: A falls by 4 and Z falls by 2, giving <sup>218</sup><sub>84</sub>Po.

items.q: A nucleus with mass number 222 and atomic number 86 emits an alpha particle. What are the mass number and atomic number of the new nucleus?
items.e: Alpha: mass −4, atomic −2. Beta: a neutron becomes a proton, so atomic +1 and mass unchanged.

items.q: A nucleus with mass number 32 and atomic number 15 emits a beta particle. What are the mass number and atomic number of the new nucleus?
items.e: Alpha: mass −4, atomic −2. Beta: a neutron becomes a proton, so atomic +1 and mass unchanged.

items.q: <sup>234</sup><sub>90</sub>Th (thorium) undergoes beta decay. What nucleus forms?
items.e: Beta decay: mass number same, atomic number +1.

items.q: <sup>214</sup><sub>82</sub>Pb (lead) undergoes beta decay. What nucleus forms?
items.e: Beta decay: mass number same, atomic number +1.

items.q: <sup>14</sup><sub>6</sub>C decays to <sup>14</sup><sub>7</sub>N. What type of decay is this?
items.e: Compare the mass numbers and atomic numbers.

items.q: <sup>226</sup><sub>88</sub>Ra decays by emitting an alpha particle. What nucleus is formed?
items.e: An alpha particle is <sup>4</sup><sub>2</sub>He: A falls by 4 and Z falls by 2, giving <sup>222</sup><sub>86</sub>Rn.

items.q: A nucleus with mass number 234 and atomic number 90 emits a beta particle. What are the mass number and atomic number of the new nucleus?
items.e: Alpha: mass −4, atomic −2. Beta: a neutron becomes a proton, so atomic +1 and mass unchanged.

items.q: <sup>238</sup><sub>92</sub>U decays by emitting an alpha particle. What nucleus is formed?
items.e: An alpha particle is <sup>4</sup><sub>2</sub>He: A falls by 4 and Z falls by 2, giving <sup>234</sup><sub>90</sub>Th.

items.q: <sup>230</sup><sub>90</sub>Th decays by emitting an alpha particle. What nucleus is formed?
items.e: An alpha particle is <sup>4</sup><sub>2</sub>He: A falls by 4 and Z falls by 2, giving <sup>226</sup><sub>88</sub>Ra.

items.q: <sup>90</sup><sub>38</sub>Sr decays by emitting a beta particle. What nucleus is formed?
items.e: In beta decay a neutron becomes a proton and an electron is emitted: A stays the same and Z rises by 1, giving <sup>90</sup><sub>39</sub>Y.

items.q: A nucleus with mass number 218 and atomic number 84 emits an alpha particle. What are the mass number and atomic number of the new nucleus?
items.e: Alpha: mass −4, atomic −2. Beta: a neutron becomes a proton, so atomic +1 and mass unchanged.

items.q: A nucleus with mass number 232 and atomic number 90 emits an alpha particle. What are the mass number and atomic number of the new nucleus?
items.e: Alpha: mass −4, atomic −2. Beta: a neutron becomes a proton, so atomic +1 and mass unchanged.

items.q: A Geiger counter reads 830 counts/min near a source, including a background count of 30 counts/min. The source's half-life is 8 years. What will the counter read after 24 years?
items.e: Subtract the background first: 800. After 3 half-lives: 100. Add the background back: 130 counts/min.

items.q: How many half-lives pass when 32 g of hydrogen-3 (tritium) decays to 1 g?
items.e: 32 g halves 5 times to reach 1 g.

items.q: What fraction of a radioactive sample remains after 3 half-lives?
items.e: Halve 3 times.

items.q: The activity of a sample falls from 800 counts/min to 50 counts/min in 32 minutes. What is the half-life?
items.e: 800 → 50 is 4 halvings, so T½ = 32 ÷ 4 = 8 minutes.

items.q: The activity of a sample falls from 3200 counts/min to 400 counts/min in 18 minutes. What is the half-life?
items.e: 3200 → 400 is 3 halvings, so T½ = 18 ÷ 3 = 6 minutes.

items.q: A Geiger counter reads 680 counts/min near a source, including a background count of 40 counts/min. The source's half-life is 20 days. What will the counter read after 80 days?
items.e: Subtract the background first: 640. After 4 half-lives: 40. Add the background back: 80 counts/min.

items.q: A Geiger counter reads 660 counts/min near a source, including a background count of 20 counts/min. The source's half-life is 6 hours. What will the counter read after 30 hours?
items.e: Subtract the background first: 640. After 5 half-lives: 20. Add the background back: 40 counts/min.

items.q: A Geiger counter reads 980 counts/min near a source, including a background count of 20 counts/min. The source's half-life is 20 hours. What will the counter read after 40 hours?
items.e: Subtract the background first: 960. After 2 half-lives: 240. Add the background back: 260 counts/min.

items.q: The activity of a sample falls from 640 counts/min to 20 counts/min in 75 days. What is the half-life?
items.e: 640 → 20 is 5 halvings, so T½ = 75 ÷ 5 = 15 days.

items.q: What fraction of a carbon-14 sample is left after 5730 years (half-life 5730 years)?
What fraction of a radioactive sample remains after 2 half-lives?
items.e: Halve 2 times.

items.q: The count rate of a sample falls from 640 to 40 counts per minute. Its half-life is 30 hours. How long did this take?
items.e: 4 half-lives.

items.q: How many half-lives pass when 400 g of caesium-137 decays to 50 g?
items.e: 400 g halves 3 times to reach 50 g.

items.q: A Geiger counter reads 430 counts/min near a source, including a background count of 30 counts/min. The source's half-life is 5 years. What will the counter read after 15 years?
items.e: Subtract the background first: 400. After 3 half-lives: 50. Add the background back: 80 counts/min.

items.q: How many half-lives pass when 80 g of cobalt-60 decays to 20 g?
items.e: 80 g halves 2 times to reach 20 g.

items.q: The count rate of a sample falls from 1600 to 400 counts per minute. Its half-life is 2 days. How long did this take?
items.e: 2 half-lives.

items.q: The count rate of a sample falls from 640 to 40 counts per minute. Its half-life is 5 minutes. How long did this take?
items.e: 4 half-lives.

items.q: The count rate of a sample falls from 1200 to 300 counts per minute. Its half-life is 30 minutes. How long did this take?
items.e: 2 half-lives.

items.q: Arjun has 480 g of hydrogen-3 (tritium) (half-life 12.3 years). How much is left after 61.5 years?
items.e: 61.5 years = 5 half-lives: 480 → 15 g.

items.q: How many half-lives pass when 16 g of hydrogen-3 (tritium) decays to 1 g?
items.e: 16 g halves 4 times to reach 1 g.

items.q: Which type of radiation is used for controlling the thickness of paper or aluminium foil?
items.e: The amount of beta getting through changes with thickness; alpha would be stopped and gamma would hardly change.

items.q: Why should radioactive sources be handled with long tongs?
c: Increasing the distance from the source reduces the exposure.
It makes the source decay faster.
items.e: Also limit time and use shielding.

items.q: <sup>60</sup><sub>27</sub>Co decays by emitting a beta particle. What nucleus is formed?
items.e: In beta decay a neutron becomes a proton and an electron is emitted: A stays the same and Z rises by 1, giving <sup>60</sup><sub>28</sub>Ni.

items.q: Which type of radiation is used for detecting leaks in underground water pipes?
items.e: A gamma tracer passes through the soil to a detector above.

items.q: Which type of radiation is used for killing cancer cells (radiotherapy) from outside the body?
items.e: Gamma can reach a tumour deep inside the body.

items.q: <sup>14</sup><sub>6</sub>C decays by emitting a beta particle. What nucleus is formed?
items.e: In beta decay a neutron becomes a proton and an electron is emitted: A stays the same and Z rises by 1, giving <sup>14</sup><sub>7</sub>N.

items.q: The activity of a sample falls from 800 counts/min to 100 counts/min in 15 years. What is the half-life?
items.e: 800 → 100 is 3 halvings, so T½ = 15 ÷ 3 = 5 years.

items.q: A Geiger counter reads 670 counts/min near a source, including a background count of 30 counts/min. The source's half-life is 5 minutes. What will the counter read after 20 minutes?
items.e: Subtract the background first: 640. After 4 half-lives: 40. Add the background back: 70 counts/min.

items.q: Why is nuclear waste stored safely for a very long time?
c: Some isotopes have very long half-lives and stay radioactive for thousands of years.
items.e: Shielded storage deep underground.

items.q: Which type of radiation is used for a medical tracer injected into the body?
items.e: Gamma passes out of the body to a detector and is weakly ionising.

items.q: What fraction of a radioactive sample remains after 5 half-lives?
items.e: After each half-life half is left: (1/2)<sup>5</sup> = 1/32.

items.q: The activity of a sample falls from 2000 counts/min to 125 counts/min in 60 years. What is the half-life?
items.e: 2000 → 125 is 4 halvings, so T½ = 60 ÷ 4 = 15 years.

items.q: The activity of a sample falls from 2000 counts/min to 250 counts/min in 45 hours. What is the half-life?
items.e: 2000 → 250 is 3 halvings, so T½ = 45 ÷ 3 = 15 hours.

items.q: A radioactive isotope has a half-life of 8 hours. How long does it take for 64 g to decay to 4 g?
items.e: 64 → 4 g is 4 half-lives: 4 × 8 = 32 hours.

items.q: Why is a gamma emitter with a short half-life chosen as a medical tracer?
c: Gamma can be detected outside the body, and the short half-life means the activity soon falls.
A short half-life makes it last for years.
items.e: Usually a half-life of hours.

items.q: Why is an alpha source safe in a smoke detector but dangerous if swallowed?
c: The detector makes it safe forever.
Alpha becomes gamma inside the body.
Outside the body, alpha cannot pass through skin; inside, it is strongly ionising and damages nearby cells.
items.e: Inside the body there is no protection.

items.q: <sup>40</sup><sub>19</sub>K decays by emitting a beta particle. What nucleus is formed?
items.e: In beta decay a neutron becomes a proton and an electron is emitted: A stays the same and Z rises by 1, giving <sup>40</sup><sub>20</sub>Ca.

items.q: Which type of radiation is used for sterilising medical instruments?
items.e: Gamma passes through the packaging and kills microorganisms.

items.q: Which type of radiation is used for a smoke detector?
items.e: Alpha particles ionise air between two plates; smoke absorbs them and the current falls, setting off the alarm.

items.q: The activity of a sample falls from 320 counts/min to 10 counts/min in 30 years. What is the half-life?
items.e: 320 → 10 is 5 halvings, so T½ = 30 ÷ 5 = 6 years.
